etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English repen, from Old English rēopan, rēpan, variants of Old English rīpan (“to reap”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīpan, from Proto-Germanic *rīpaną (compare West Frisian repe, Norwegian ripa (“to score, scratch”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyb- (“to snatch”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cut (for example a grain) with a sickle, scythe, or reaping machine
(transitive) To gather (e.g. a harvest) by cutting.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Leviticus 19:9:
quote.text: And when ye reape the haruest of your land, thou shalt not wholly reape the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy haruest.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To obtain or receive as a reward, in a good or a bad sense.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Galatians 6:7:
quote.text: Be not deceiued, God is not mocked: for whatsoeuer a man soweth, that shall he also reape.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 60:
quote.text: Why do I humble thus my ſelf, and ſuing / For peace, reap nothing but repulſe and hate?

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XLI, page 64:
quote.text: And what delights can equal those⁠That stir the spirit’s inner deeps,⁠When one that loves but knows not, reapsA truth from one that loves and knows?

quote.citation: 2016 June 11, Phil McNulty, “England 1-1 Russia”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: England manager Roy Hodgson got plenty right with a positive selection and the decision to play Rooney in midfield reaped a rich reward - but his boldest move may also have been his biggest mistake.

definitions.definition: (transitive, computer science) To terminate a child process that has previously exited, thereby removing it from the process table.
(transitive, obsolete) To deprive of the beard; to shave.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Came there a certaine Lord, neat and trimly drest;Fresh as a Bride-groome, and his Chin new reapt,

definitions.definition: A bundle of grain; a handful of grain laid down by the reaper as it is cut.
